Pathology-01.question: ১) Atrophy occurs when-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is decreased nutrients and decreased stimulation. Atrophy is a decrease in the size of a cell, tissue, or organ due to reduced workload, reduced hormonal stimulation, poor nutrition, or loss of nerve supply.

Common causes of atrophy:

  • ↓ Nutrient supply (starvation, cachexia)

  • ↓ Hormonal stimulation (e.g., endometrial atrophy after menopause)

  • ↓ Workload (disuse atrophy)

  • Loss of nerve supply (denervation atrophy)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Altered physiologic stimuli → Can cause adaptation, but not specifically atrophy.

  • Increased demand, increased stimulation → Causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia.

  • Chronic irritation (physical or chemical) → Causes metaplasia.

High-yield points:

Cellular adaptations:

Stimulus Adaptation
↓ Workload / ↓ nutrients / ↓ stimulation Atrophy
↑ Workload Hypertrophy
↑ Hormonal stimulation Hyperplasia
Chronic irritation Metaplasia

Exam pearl:
Atrophy = decreased cell size due to decreased demand, nutrients, or stimulation.

Pathology-01.question: ২) An increase in their number of cells
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is hyperplasia. Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ due to increased cell proliferation.

Examples:

  • Physiological:

    • Enlargement of uterus during pregnancy (hormonal hyperplasia)

    • Breast glandular proliferation during puberty

  • Pathological:

    • Endometrial hyperplasia due to excess oestrogen

    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypertrophy – Increase in cell size, not cell number (e.g., skeletal muscle enlargement).

  • Atrophy – Decrease in cell size and organ size.

  • Metaplasia – Reversible change from one mature cell type to another.

High-yield points:

Adaptation Change
Hyperplasia ↑ Number of cells
Hypertrophy ↑ Size of cells
Atrophy ↓ Size of cells
Metaplasia Change in cell type

Exam pearl:
More cells = Hyperplasia; bigger cells = Hypertrophy.

Pathology-01.question: ৩) Time (in minute) for autoclaving
৪) Surgical gowns are sterilized by
৫) Which one is the hallmark of malignancy?
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is metastasis. Metastasis (spread of malignant cells to distant, non-contiguous sites) is considered the hallmark feature of malignancy.

Mechanism:

  • Tumour cells invade surrounding tissue

  • Enter blood or lymphatic vessels

  • Establish secondary tumours at distant sites

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Rapid growth – Can occur in both benign and malignant tumours; not specific.

  • Anaplasia – A feature of malignant tumours showing loss of cellular differentiation, but not the defining hallmark.

  • Local invasion – Common in malignancy, but metastasis is the most characteristic feature distinguishing malignant from benign tumours.

High-yield points:

Features of malignancy:

  • Anaplasia

  • Increased mitosis

  • Local invasion

  • Metastasis (hallmark)

Exam pearl:
Benign tumours do not metastasize; metastasis = definitive evidence of malignancy.

Pathology-01.question: ৬) Pathological hypertrophy occurs in-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is heart. Cardiac hypertrophy is a classic example of pathological hypertrophy caused by increased workload.

Examples:

  • Hypertension → left ventricular hypertrophy

  • Aortic stenosis → pressure overload → cardiac hypertrophy

The other options are incorrect because they represent physiological hypertrophy:

  • Skeletal muscle hypertrophy – Due to exercise/training.

  • Pregnant uterus – Due to hormonal stimulation and increased workload.

  • Lactating breasts – Mainly due to physiological hormonal changes causing glandular enlargement.

High-yield points:

Hypertrophy = ↑ cell size (not number)

Type Example
Physiological hypertrophy Skeletal muscle, pregnant uterus
Pathological hypertrophy Heart in hypertension/aortic stenosis

Exam pearl:
Heart enlargement due to pressure overload = pathological hypertrophy.

Pathology-01.question: ৭) Oncogenic bacteria
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Helicobacter pylori. It is an oncogenic bacterium associated with:

  • Gastric adenocarcinoma

  • MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) lymphoma

Mechanism:

  • Chronic gastritis → mucosal damage → atrophy → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → carcinoma

The other options are incorrect because:

  • C. jejuni – Causes gastroenteritis and is associated with Guillain–Barré syndrome, not a major oncogenic bacterium.

  • B. anthracis – Causes anthrax.

  • B. coli (Balantidium coli) – Causes intestinal infection; not oncogenic.

High-yield points:

Important oncogenic infections:

  • H. pylori → Gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

  • HPV → Cervical cancer

  • EBV → Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma

  • HBV/HCV → Hepatocellular carcinoma

Exam pearl:
Only major oncogenic bacteria = H. pylori.

Pathology-01.question: ৮) Grading of cancer is based on
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is degree of differentiation. Cancer grading describes the microscopic appearance and biological aggressiveness of a tumour, mainly based on how closely tumour cells resemble normal cells.

Features assessed:

  • Degree of differentiation

  • Cellular atypia (anaplasia)

  • Mitotic activity

The other options are incorrect because they relate to staging, not grading:

  • Tumour size → Part of TNM staging (T)

  • Nodal involvement → Part of TNM staging (N)

  • Metastasis → Part of TNM staging (M)

High-yield points:

Grading vs Staging:

Feature Based on
Grade Cell differentiation & microscopic appearance
Stage Tumour size, lymph nodes, metastasis (TNM)

Exam pearl:
Grade = differentiation; Stage = TNM spread.

Pathology-01.question: ৯) Hypertrophy + Hyperplasia simultaneously occurs in following organ except-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is penis. Simultaneous hypertrophy and hyperplasia occur in some organs where enlargement involves both increase in cell size and cell number, but this is not a feature of the penis.

Examples:

  • Thyroid – Enlargement in some goitres involves follicular cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia.

  • Breast – During pregnancy, hormonal stimulation causes ductal and glandular hyperplasia with cellular hypertrophy.

  • Prostate – Benign prostatic hyperplasia involves proliferation of glandular and stromal components (hyperplasia).

  • Penis – Enlargement is mainly due to growth and structural changes, not a classic example of combined hypertrophy and hyperplasia.

High-yield points:

Hypertrophy + Hyperplasia examples:

  • Pregnancy uterus (classic)

  • Breast during pregnancy

  • Some endocrine organ enlargements

Exam pearl:
Penis is not a typical organ showing combined hypertrophy and hyperplasia.

Pathology-01.question: ১০) The first manifestation of almost all forms of injury to cells is
Pathology-01.option2: Plasma membrane alterations, such as blebbing, blunting,
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is cellular swelling. It is the earliest and most common manifestation of reversible cell injury.

Mechanism:

  • Cellular injury → ↓ ATP production

  • Failure of Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase pump

  • Na⁺ and water enter the cell

  • Cell swelling occurs (hydropic change)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Plasma membrane alterations (blebbing, blunting) – Occur in reversible injury but are later ultrastructural changes.

  • Loss of microvilli – An early membrane change, but not the first general manifestation.

  • Mitochondrial changes – Occur early but follow disruption of cellular energy metabolism.

High-yield points:

First sign of reversible cell injury:
→ Cellular swelling (hydropic degeneration)

Reversible injury features:

  • Cellular swelling

  • Fatty change

  • Membrane blebbing

  • Loss of microvilli

  • Mitochondrial swelling

Exam pearl:
Earliest manifestation of almost all cell injury = Cellular swelling.

Pathology-01.question: ১১) Wilms tumour is a malignant tumour of
১২) Criteria of benign tumour
১৩) Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma is associated with
১৪) CA 19-9 is related to carcinoma of
১৫) Which type of tumour mainly follows lymphatic spread?
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is carcinoma. Carcinomas mainly spread through lymphatic vessels because they arise from epithelial tissues, which have rich lymphatic drainage.

Examples:

  • Breast carcinoma → axillary lymph nodes

  • Lung carcinoma → mediastinal lymph nodes

  • Gastric carcinoma → regional lymph nodes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Sarcoma – Malignant tumour of mesenchymal tissue; spreads mainly through the bloodstream (haematogenous spread).

  • Adenoma – Benign glandular tumour; does not metastasize.

  • Fibroma – Benign fibrous tissue tumour; does not metastasize.

High-yield points:

Routes of tumour spread:

Tumour type Main spread
Carcinoma Lymphatic spread
Sarcoma Haematogenous spread
Melanoma Both lymphatic and blood

Exam pearl:
Carcinoma → lymphatics; sarcoma → blood.

Pathology-01.question: ১৬) Prevention of ROS production by free copper molecule done by -
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is ceruloplasmin. Free copper ions (Cu⁺/Cu²⁺) can participate in redox reactions and generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) through free radical formation. Ceruloplasmin binds copper and prevents this toxic activity.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Transferrin – Binds and transports iron (Fe³⁺) in plasma; reduces free iron-mediated ROS.

  • Ferritin – Stores intracellular iron and prevents iron-induced oxidative damage.

  • Lactoferrin – Binds iron in secretions (e.g., milk, tears) and has antimicrobial activity.

High-yield points:

Metal-binding proteins:

  • Ceruloplasmin → Copper transport + prevents copper toxicity

  • Transferrin → Plasma iron transport

  • Ferritin → Intracellular iron storage

  • Lactoferrin → Iron binding in secretions

Exam pearl:
Free copper → ROS prevention = Ceruloplasmin.

Pathology-01.question: ১৭) Enzyme not involve in removal of free radical
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is dehydrogenase. Dehydrogenases are mainly involved in oxidation–reduction reactions and metabolism, but they are not major antioxidant enzymes responsible for removing free radicals.

The major enzymes involved in free radical removal are:

  • Superoxide dismutase (SOD)
    → Converts superoxide radicals (O₂⁻) into hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)

  • Catalase
    → Converts H₂O₂ into water and oxygen

  • Glutathione peroxidase
    → Removes H₂O₂ and lipid peroxides using glutathione

The other options are incorrect because they are antioxidant enzymes.

High-yield points:

Antioxidant enzymes:

  1. Superoxide dismutase → O₂⁻ → H₂O₂

  2. Catalase → H₂O₂ → H₂O + O₂

  3. Glutathione peroxidase → H₂O₂/lipid peroxide removal

Exam pearl:
Dehydrogenase is not a free radical scavenging enzyme.

Pathology-01.question: ১৮) Criteria of acute inflammation
১৯) Molecules involved in ARDS
২০) Which metabolite of arachidonic acid increases vascular permeability?
২১) Derived from dendritic cell
২২) Disinfection of skin prior to blood culture
২৩) Mediators of fever excludes
২৪) Reactive oxygen species is a mediator of
২৫) Gumma is found in
২৬) Type of necrosis in abscess-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is liquefactive necrosis. An abscess is a localized collection of pus caused by infection, and the tissue destruction occurs mainly through liquefactive necrosis.

Mechanism:

  • Neutrophil infiltration

  • Release of lysosomal enzymes

  • Digestion of dead cells → liquid pus formation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Coagulative necrosis – Typical of ischemic infarction in solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen).

  • Caseous necrosis – Seen in tuberculosis and some fungal infections.

  • Fat necrosis – Seen in acute pancreatitis and traumatic injury to fatty tissue.

High-yield points:

Type of necrosis Example
Liquefactive Abscess, brain infarct
Coagulative Myocardial infarction
Caseous Tuberculosis
Fat necrosis Acute pancreatitis

Exam pearl:
Abscess → Liquefactive necrosis.

Pathology-01.question: ২৭) Pathway of cell death that is induced by a tightly regulated suicide program -
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is apoptosis. Apoptosis is a form of programmed cell death controlled by a tightly regulated intracellular suicide program.

Features of apoptosis:

  • Energy-dependent process

  • Regulated by caspases

  • Cell shrinkage

  • Nuclear fragmentation

  • Formation of apoptotic bodies

  • Minimal inflammation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Necrosis – Uncontrolled cell death due to severe injury; associated with inflammation.

  • Necroptosis – Regulated form of necrotic cell death with necrosis-like features, but not the classic programmed suicide pathway.

  • Pyroptosis – Inflammatory programmed cell death mediated by inflammasomes and caspase-1, commonly during infection.

High-yield points:

Cell death Main feature
Apoptosis Tightly regulated programmed cell death
Necrosis Uncontrolled injury-related death
Necroptosis Regulated necrotic death
Pyroptosis Inflammatory cell death

Exam pearl:
"Programmed cellular suicide" = Apoptosis.

Pathology-01.question: ২৮) Necroptosis occurs in-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is all of above. Necroptosis is a form of regulated necrotic cell death that occurs in several pathological conditions, including:

  • Steatohepatitis → hepatocyte injury with necroptotic pathways

  • Acute pancreatitis → acinar cell injury and inflammatory necroptosis

  • Reperfusion injury → ROS and inflammatory pathways trigger necroptosis

Mechanism:

  • Mediated by RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL proteins

  • Causes membrane disruption and inflammation, resembling necrosis

The other options are incorrect because each listed condition can involve necroptosis.

High-yield points:

Cell death type Key feature
Apoptosis Caspase-mediated, non-inflammatory
Necroptosis RIPK1/RIPK3/MLKL-mediated regulated necrosis
Pyroptosis Inflammasome + caspase-1 mediated inflammatory death
Necrosis Unregulated injury-related death

Exam pearl:
Necroptosis is seen in steatohepatitis, acute pancreatitis, and ischemia–reperfusion injury

Pathology-01.question: ২৯) Cardinal signs of inflammation ‘calor’ means: -
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Heat. Calor is one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation and refers to increased local temperature (heat).

The five cardinal signs of inflammation:

Latin term Meaning
Rubor Redness
Calor Heat
Tumor Swelling
Dolor Pain
Functio laesa Loss of function

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Redness → Rubor

  • Swelling → Tumor

  • Pain → Dolor

Exam pearl:
Calor = Heat.

Pathology-01.question: ৩০) Mediators of pain-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is bradykinin. Bradykinin is one of the most important mediators of pain in acute inflammation by stimulating nociceptors.

Major actions:

  • Causes pain

  • Increases vascular permeability

  • Causes vasodilation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IL-1 – Mainly mediates fever and leukocyte activation.

  • TNF – Causes endothelial activation, inflammation, and systemic effects.

  • Prostaglandins (especially PGE₂) – Sensitize nerve endings and enhance pain, but bradykinin is the primary pain mediator.

High-yield points:

Inflammatory effect Major mediator
Pain Bradykinin, PGE₂
Fever IL-1, TNF, IL-6, PGE₂
Vasodilation Histamine, NO, prostaglandins
↑ Vascular permeability Histamine, LTC₄/D₄/E₄

Exam pearl:
Classical mediator of pain in inflammation = Bradykinin

Pathology-01.question: ৩১) Caseating granuloma produce in-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is tuberculosis. Caseating granuloma is the classic histopathological feature of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.

Features:

  • Central caseous (cheese-like) necrosis

  • Surrounding epithelioid cells

  • Langhans giant cells

  • Rim of lymphocytes

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Leprosy – Causes granulomatous inflammation but typically non-caseating granulomas (especially tuberculoid type).

  • Syphilis – Produces gumma (tertiary syphilis), not caseating granuloma.

  • Cat-scratch disease – Causes stellate necrotizing granulomas with suppurative features.

High-yield points:

Disease Granuloma type
Tuberculosis Caseating granuloma
Sarcoidosis Non-caseating granuloma
Syphilis Gumma
Cat-scratch disease Stellate necrotizing granuloma

Exam pearl:
Caseous necrosis + granuloma = Tuberculosis.

Pathology-01.question: ৩২) Which one is double edged sword?
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is metaplasia. Metaplasia is considered a double-edged sword because it is an adaptive, protective change but may increase the risk of malignant transformation if the stimulus persists.

Example:

  • Smoking → respiratory epithelium changes from columnar ciliated epithelium to stratified squamous epithelium

  • Persistent irritation → dysplasia → squamous cell carcinoma risk

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Atrophy – Adaptive decrease in cell size due to reduced workload or stimulation.

  • Hypertrophy – Increase in cell size due to increased workload; may become harmful if excessive (e.g., cardiac hypertrophy), but not classically called a double-edged sword.

  • Hyperplasia – Increase in cell number; can be physiological or pathological, but the classic "double-edged sword" term refers to metaplasia.

High-yield points:

Metaplasia:

  • Reversible adaptive change

  • Protects against stress

  • Can predispose to cancer

Exam pearl:
Metaplasia = protective adaptation + risk of malignancy → double-edged sword.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৩) Metaplasia from squamous to columnar type may also occur in
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Barrett oesophagus. It is an example of squamous epithelium changing to columnar epithelium due to chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Mechanism:

  • Chronic acid reflux damages normal stratified squamous epithelium of the lower oesophagus.

  • It is replaced by columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia.

  • Increases risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Aphthous ulcer – Causes mucosal ulceration, commonly seen in Crohn’s disease; not metaplasia.

  • MALToma – A type of lymphoma associated with chronic inflammation (e.g., H. pylori), not epithelial metaplasia.

  • Oesophageal varices – Dilated veins due to portal hypertension; no epithelial transformation.

High-yield points:

Types of metaplasia:

  • Squamous → Columnar: Barrett oesophagus

  • Columnar → Squamous: chronic irritation in some glandular tissues

Exam pearl:
Barrett oesophagus = intestinal columnar metaplasia replacing squamous epithelium.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৪) Ischemic necrosis of heart indicates which type of necrosis?
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is coagulative necrosis. Ischemic necrosis of solid organs, including the heart, typically produces coagulative necrosis.

Mechanism:

  • Ischaemia causes protein denaturation.

  • Cellular architecture is preserved initially despite cell death.

  • The tissue becomes firm and pale.

Examples:

  • Myocardial infarction

  • Renal infarction

  • Splenic infarction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Liquefactive necrosis – Seen in abscesses and brain infarction.

  • Caseous necrosis – Characteristic of tuberculosis.

  • Fibrinoid necrosis – Seen in immune-mediated vascular injury (e.g., vasculitis) and malignant hypertension.

High-yield points:

Type of necrosis Classic example
Coagulative Myocardial infarction
Liquefactive Abscess, brain infarct
Caseous TB
Fibrinoid Vasculitis

Exam pearl:
Ischaemic necrosis of heart = Coagulative necrosis.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৫) Traumatic fat necrosis occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is breast. Traumatic fat necrosis commonly occurs in the breast following blunt trauma or injury.

Mechanism:

  • Trauma damages adipocytes

  • Fat cells rupture → release lipid

  • Lipid triggers inflammatory response

  • May form a firm lump that can mimic breast carcinoma clinically

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Uterus – Not a typical site of traumatic fat necrosis.

  • Kidney – Ischemic injury causes coagulative necrosis.

  • Pancreas – Causes enzymatic fat necrosis in acute pancreatitis (saponification).

High-yield points:

Types of fat necrosis:

  • Traumatic fat necrosis → Breast

  • Enzymatic fat necrosis → Acute pancreatitis

Exam pearl:
Breast lump after trauma = traumatic fat necrosis.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৬) In apoptosis
৩৭) superoxide is inactivated by
৩৮) Local factors that influence tissue repair
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is infection. Infection is a local factor that influences tissue repair by causing persistent inflammation, tissue destruction, and delayed healing.

Factors affecting tissue repair:

Local factors:

  • Infection (most important local factor)

  • Mechanical stress

  • Foreign bodies

  • Poor blood supply

Systemic factors:

  • Diabetes mellitus

  • Nutritional status

  • Glucocorticoids (steroids)

  • Age

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Diabetes → Systemic factor that delays wound healing.

  • Glucocorticoids (steroids) → Systemic factor; inhibit inflammation and collagen synthesis.

  • Nutritional status → Systemic factor; protein and vitamin deficiencies impair repair.

High-yield points:

Type Examples
Local factors Infection, mechanical stress, blood supply, foreign bodies
Systemic factors Diabetes, nutrition, steroids, age

Exam pearl:
Most important local factor delaying tissue repair = Infection.

Pathology-01.question: ৩৯) Virchow triad include-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is all of the above. Virchow triad describes the three major factors responsible for thrombosis formation:

  1. Endothelial injury

    • Most important in arterial thrombosis

    • Exposes subendothelial collagen → platelet activation

  2. Abnormal blood flow

    • Includes stasis and turbulence

    • Promotes platelet contact with endothelium and clot formation

  3. Hypercoagulability of blood

    • Increased tendency of blood to clot

    • Can be inherited or acquired

The other options are individually correct but incomplete.

High-yield points:

Virchow triad:

  • Endothelial injury

  • Abnormal blood flow (stasis/turbulence)

  • Hypercoagulability

Exam pearl:
All three components together form Virchow triad.

Pathology-01.question: ৪০) Malignant tumor of skeletal muscle-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is rhabdomyosarcoma. It is a malignant tumour of skeletal muscle arising from skeletal muscle differentiation cells.

Key points:

  • Common in children and adolescents

  • Associated with skeletal muscle lineage

  • Common sites:

    • Head and neck

    • Genitourinary tract

    • Extremities

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Chondrosarcoma → Malignant tumour of cartilage.

  • Osteogenic sarcoma (osteosarcoma) → Malignant tumour of bone-forming cells (osteoblasts).

  • Angiosarcoma → Malignant tumour of vascular endothelial cells.

High-yield points:

Tumour Tissue of origin
Rhabdomyosarcoma Skeletal muscle
Osteosarcoma Bone
Chondrosarcoma Cartilage
Angiosarcoma Blood vessels

Exam pearl:
Skeletal muscle malignancy = Rhabdomyosarcoma.

Pathology-01.question: ৪১) Hepatic angiosarcoma associated with-
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is vinyl chloride. Hepatic angiosarcoma is classically associated with exposure to vinyl chloride, used in the manufacture of polyvinyl chloride (PVC).

Other important associations:

  • Thorotrast (thorium dioxide) → Hepatic angiosarcoma

  • Arsenic → Hepatic angiosarcoma

  • Anabolic steroids → Hepatic tumours (especially adenoma)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Arsenic – Also associated with hepatic angiosarcoma, but the classic exam association is vinyl chloride.

  • Beryllium – Associated with chronic granulomatous lung disease (berylliosis), not hepatic angiosarcoma.

  • Radon – Associated mainly with lung cancer.

High-yield points:

Carcinogen–tumour associations:

Exposure Tumour
Vinyl chloride Hepatic angiosarcoma
Thorotrast Hepatic angiosarcoma
Benzene Acute myeloid leukaemia
Asbestos Mesothelioma
Aflatoxin B1 Hepatocellular carcinoma

Exam pearl:
Vinyl chloride → Hepatic angiosarcoma.

Pathology-01.question: ৪২) Guardian of the Genome
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is TP53. TP53 gene encodes the p53 protein, known as the “guardian of the genome” because it maintains genomic stability by preventing the propagation of damaged DNA.

Functions of p53:

  • Detects DNA damage

  • Causes cell cycle arrest (mainly at G1/S checkpoint)

  • Allows DNA repair

  • Induces apoptosis if damage is irreparable

The other options are incorrect because:

  • APC – Tumour suppressor gene associated with colorectal carcinoma (familial adenomatous polyposis).

  • RB – Regulates G1 → S phase transition; known as the “gatekeeper of the cell cycle.”

  • VHL – Tumour suppressor gene associated with renal cell carcinoma and VHL syndrome.

High-yield points:

Gene Key association
TP53 Guardian of the genome
RB Gatekeeper of cell cycle
APC Colorectal cancer
VHL Clear cell renal carcinoma

Exam pearl:
Guardian of genome = TP53 (p53).

Pathology-01.question: ৪৩) CA-15-3 tumour marker of
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is breast cancer. CA 15-3 is a tumour marker mainly associated with breast carcinoma, especially for monitoring treatment response and recurrence.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ovarian cancer → Mainly associated with CA-125.

  • Colon cancer → Mainly associated with CEA (carcinoembryonic antigen).

  • Pancreatic cancer → Mainly associated with CA 19-9.

High-yield tumour markers:

Tumour marker Associated cancer
CA 15-3 Breast cancer
CA-125 Ovarian cancer
CEA Colorectal cancer
CA 19-9 Pancreatic cancer
AFP Hepatocellular carcinoma

Exam pearl:
CA 15-3 = Breast carcinoma.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৪) Which is excess production of scar tissue that is out of proportion to the wound?
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is keloid. A keloid is an excessive production of scar tissue (collagen) that extends beyond the original wound margins and is disproportionate to the initial injury.

Features of keloid:

  • Excessive collagen deposition

  • Extends beyond wound boundaries

  • Does not regress spontaneously

  • Common in darker skin types

  • Common sites: earlobe, shoulder, chest

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypertrophic scar – Excess scar tissue but remains within the original wound boundaries and may regress over time.

  • Wound dehiscence – Separation or reopening of a wound due to failure of repair.

  • Naevus – A benign melanocytic lesion (mole), unrelated to scar formation.

High-yield points:

Condition Key feature
Keloid Scar extends beyond wound margin
Hypertrophic scar Scar confined within wound margin
Dehiscence Wound separation

Exam pearl:
Excess scar tissue beyond wound = Keloid.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৫) Cumulative sub lethal injury over long life span causes
৪৬) The most common stimulus for hypertrophy of muscle is
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is increased workload. The most common stimulus for muscle hypertrophy is an increased functional demand placed on the muscle.

Mechanism:

  • Increased workload → mechanical stress → increased synthesis of structural proteins → enlargement of individual muscle fibres

Examples:

  • Weight training → skeletal muscle hypertrophy

  • Hypertension/aortic stenosis → cardiac hypertrophy

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Decreased workload → Causes atrophy (e.g., disuse atrophy).

  • Change in tissue type → Causes metaplasia.

  • Unexpected tissue death → Leads to necrosis/inflammation, not hypertrophy.

High-yield points:

Cellular adaptations:

  • ↑ Workload → Hypertrophy

  • ↓ Workload → Atrophy

  • Chronic irritation → Metaplasia

  • ↑ Cell number → Hyperplasia

Exam pearl:
Most common stimulus for hypertrophy = Increased workload.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৭) Key mediator of swelling in acute inflammation
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is Histamine. Histamine is the key mediator responsible for swelling (tumor) in acute inflammation by causing increased vascular permeability of post-capillary venules.

Mechanism:

  • Histamine released from mast cells, basophils, and platelets

  • Causes endothelial cell contraction

  • Produces gaps between endothelial cells

  • → Plasma protein and fluid leakage (exudation)

  • → Swelling (oedema)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Bradykinin – Mainly mediates pain and also increases vascular permeability.

  • Prostaglandins – Mainly cause vasodilation, pain, and fever.

  • Prostacyclin (PGI₂) – Causes vasodilation and inhibits platelet aggregation.

High-yield points:

Inflammatory sign Major mediator
Swelling (oedema) Histamine
Pain Bradykinin, PGE₂
Fever IL-1, TNF, IL-6, PGE₂
Vasodilation Histamine, NO, prostaglandins

Exam pearl:
Acute inflammation swelling = Histamine-mediated increased vascular permeability.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৮) Pathological hypertrophy occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is myocardium. Cardiac hypertrophy is a classic example of pathological hypertrophy caused by increased workload or stress.

Examples:

  • Hypertension → pressure overload → left ventricular hypertrophy

  • Aortic stenosis → pressure overload → myocardial hypertrophy

The other options are examples of physiological hypertrophy:

  • Uterus → Enlarges during pregnancy due to hormonal stimulation and increased workload.

  • Breast → Enlargement during pregnancy and lactation due to hormonal stimulation.

  • Skeletal muscle → Enlarges with exercise and increased workload.

High-yield points:

Type Example
Pathological hypertrophy Myocardium in hypertension
Physiological hypertrophy Skeletal muscle, pregnant uterus, breast

Exam pearl:
Heart enlargement due to disease = pathological hypertrophy.

Pathology-01.question: ৪৯) Cell number is increased in
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is hyperplasia. Hyperplasia is an increase in the number of cells in a tissue or organ due to increased cell proliferation.

Examples:

  • Physiological hyperplasia:

    • Breast glandular proliferation during pregnancy

    • Regeneration of liver after partial hepatectomy

  • Pathological hyperplasia:

    • Endometrial hyperplasia

    • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hypertrophy → Increase in cell size, not number.

  • Atrophy → Decrease in cell size and organ size.

  • Metaplasia → Reversible change from one mature cell type to another.

High-yield points:

Adaptation Change
Hyperplasia ↑ Number of cells
Hypertrophy ↑ Cell size
Atrophy ↓ Cell size
Metaplasia Change in cell type

Exam pearl:
Increase in cell number = Hyperplasia.

Pathology-01.question: ৫০) Which one is age related atrophy?
Pathology-01.exp:
The correct answer is senile atrophy. Age-related atrophy is known as senile atrophy, which occurs due to the natural ageing process.

Examples:

  • Brain atrophy in elderly individuals

  • Reduction in muscle mass with ageing (sarcopenia)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Pressure atrophy → Due to prolonged pressure causing tissue compression (e.g., pressure on bone by a tumour).

  • Denervation atrophy → Due to loss of nerve supply to muscle.

  • Disuse atrophy → Due to decreased workload or immobilization (e.g., limb immobilization).

High-yield points:

Types of atrophy:

  • Senile → Age-related

  • Disuse → Reduced activity

  • Denervation → Loss of nerve supply

  • Pressure → Compression

Exam pearl:
Age-related atrophy = Senile atrophy.
